presentingComplaint: Sudden severe abdominal and back pain with a brief collapse
history: A 74-year-old man was brought to the emergency department after sudden-onset, tearing central abdominal pain radiating through to the lower back and left flank while at rest, followed by a transient loss of consciousness at home. He is a lifelong smoker (50 pack-years) with long-standing hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus on metformin and insulin, and stage 3b chronic kidney disease (baseline creatinine 1.9 mg/dL) followed in the renal clinic. Because of the flank radiation and known CKD, the referring GP initially queried ureteric (renal) colic. He has never had documented aortic imaging. There is no fever, dysuria, vomiting or preceding trauma. He takes ramipril, atorvastatin, aspirin, metformin and insulin. On arrival he is pale, clammy and restless with ongoing pain despite opioids.
examination: Pale, diaphoretic, in distress. Abdomen soft but with a tender, expansile pulsatile mass palpable in the epigastrium/periumbilical region; left flank fullness and tenderness. Peripheries cool with delayed capillary refill; femoral pulses present but thready. No costovertebral angle percussion tenderness reproducing a colic pattern. No peritonism initially. Chest clear, heart sounds normal with no murmur. GCS 15 after the syncopal episode but anxious.
imaging: Bedside point-of-care ultrasound of the aorta shows an infrarenal abdominal aorta measuring 7.4 cm with surrounding hypoechoic retroperitoneal fluid. CT angiogram of the aorta (performed rapidly given haemodynamic instability, accepting contrast-nephropathy risk in CKD as life-threatening rupture takes precedence) confirms a 7.5 cm infrarenal AAA with active contrast extravasation and a left retroperitoneal haematoma. No aortic dissection flap; renal arteries patent, no obstructing ureteric calculus.
microbiology: Not applicable — non-infective vascular emergency; no cultures indicated.
differentialDiagnoses: Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm (leading — pulsatile expansile mass, hypotension, retroperitoneal haematoma on imaging)
Aortic dissection (tearing pain radiating to back; excluded — no intimal flap, aneurysmal sac with extravasation instead)
Ureteric/renal colic (flank pain + CKD initially suggested this; no obstructing calculus, no true haematuria)
Acute mesenteric ischaemia (pain out of proportion; excluded by CT)
Acute pancreatitis (epigastric/back pain; lipase not consistent, CT shows aortic pathology)
finalDiagnosis: Ruptured infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm with haemorrhagic (hypovolaemic) shock and acute-on-chronic kidney injury, in a patient with type 2 diabetes and CKD.
citations: Society for Vascular Surgery — Care of Patients with Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm — 2018
European Society for Vascular Surgery (ESVS) — Clinical Practice Guidelines on the Management of Abdominal Aorto-iliac Artery Aneurysms — 2019
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Diseases of the Aorta
stewardship: Not applicable — ruptured AAA is a non-infective surgical vascular emergency. No empiric antibiotics are indicated for the rupture itself; antibiotics are limited to standard peri-operative surgical prophylaxis at the time of repair. Management priorities are immediate vascular-surgery activation, permissive hypotension (target SBP ~70-90 mmHg / palpable radial pulse, avoiding aggressive crystalloid), activation of massive transfusion protocol, and emergent EVAR or open repair for definitive source control.
contraindications: Avoid aggressive fluid/crystalloid resuscitation to normal BP before repair — practise permissive/hypotensive resuscitation to limit clot disruption and rebleeding
Do not delay definitive imaging/repair to correct contrast-nephropathy risk in CKD — rupture is immediately life-threatening
Avoid nephrotoxins (NSAIDs) and hold metformin (lactic acidosis / contrast) and ACE inhibitor given AKI and shock
edgeCases: Flank pain radiation plus known CKD can anchor clinicians on renal colic and delay diagnosis
Diabetic autonomic neuropathy and beta-adrenergic blunting may mask the expected tachycardic/hypertensive response
Baseline CKD elevates creatinine, so acute-on-chronic AKI from hypoperfusion may be underestimated
A transiently 'stable' contained rupture can decompensate abruptly during transfer or imaging
expectedMaiK: Sudden abdominal/back pain + syncope + a pulsatile expansile abdominal mass + hypotension in an elderly arteriopath is a ruptured AAA until proven otherwise; secure large-bore access, activate vascular surgery and massive transfusion, use permissive hypotension, and do not let CKD/renal-colic framing delay emergent CT angiogram and repair.
expectedNextQuestions: Character, onset and radiation of the pain, and any prior known aortic aneurysm or aortic imaging
Was the collapse a true syncope, and any ongoing anticoagulant/antiplatelet use?
Smoking, hypertension and vascular disease history
Baseline renal function and last known creatinine
Time of last oral intake and code/frailty status for emergency surgery
expectedInvestigations: CT angiogram of the aorta (if haemodynamics permit)
Urgent group & crossmatch (≥4 units) and coagulation screen
FBC, U&E/creatinine, venous lactate and blood gas
regressionAssertions: Engine returns aaa as the top diagnosis
No empiric antibiotics recommended (non-infective; stewardship tier null)
Pulsatile abdominal mass + hypotension + syncope flagged as ruptured-AAA red flags
